title: The Phasing Call
primary_metric: hours of autonomous-flight/consumables reserve remaining at docking per calendar day of launch-window phase-angle flexibility gained

options.A: The Fast-Track — a direct, few-orbit rendezvous profile that reaches the station fastest and preserves the most autonomous-flight/consumables reserve, at the cost of a narrow launch-window phase-angle tolerance
options.B: The Phasing Climb — a multi-orbit parking-orbit phasing rendezvous profile that tolerates the widest range of launch-day phase angles, at the cost of spending far more of the vehicle's fixed reserve reaching the station

_ext: keys below are pipeline extensions, additive to SPEC §4
protagonist: Talia Brooks, Trajectory Analyst, Meridian Launch Systems

replaces.reason: the-transfer-window's balance test failed by ~800x (margin_pct=15940.5), a fixed, structural chemical-vs-electric-propulsion transit-time asymmetry that cannot be retuned without fabricating a number (see cases/the-transfer-window/RESEARCH_LOG.md, 'RETUNE PASS — 2026-08-31'). the-transfer-window is left unmodified as the historical record. This case keeps the same protagonist/career/company/skill group and swaps the deciding asymmetry to a same-propulsion-system rendezvous-timing-strategy comparison, which real precedent shows differs by a realistic few-x, not several-hundred-x.

deliverables.text: A conversion of the client station's tracked position (Appendix A) from the polar coordinate its tracking radar reports -- a bearing and range from the tracking site -- into a rectangular coordinate, with your conversion work shown in full.

A pair of parametric position equations, x(t) and y(t), for each rendezvous profile (the Fast-Track and the Phasing Climb), using each profile's stated angular catch-up rate from Appendix B, with the parameter identified by name and explained in plain terms (what it represents physically, and what values it ranges over for each profile's full rendezvous).

For each profile, the rectangular (Cartesian) equation of the vehicle's closing path, found by eliminating the parameter from that profile's D2 equations, showing every algebraic step -- followed by a solved check, using that rectangular equation, of the elapsed time at which each profile actually reaches the station's D1 rectangular position, with your algebra shown in full.

An autonomous-flight/consumables-reserve calculation for each profile: what percent of Appendix C's fixed total allowance is used up by the time each profile reaches docking (using your D3 elapsed-transit-time figures), and what percent remains as reserve.

A graphed polar boundary for each profile's phase-angle tolerance band (Appendix D): using the 0-360 degree phase-angle circle centered on the moment of liftoff, graph each profile's workable phase-angle band as a polar equation, stating that equation explicitly, so the two bands' relative widths are visible on a single polar plot.

A launch-window calendar calculation for each profile: using your D5 graphed phase-angle bands and the station's orbital period from Appendix D, how many days in a 30-day launch calendar fall inside each profile's workable phase-angle window, with your arithmetic shown.

A single primary-metric comparison table -- hours of reserve margin remaining at docking (from D4) per calendar day of launch-window flexibility (from D6) -- built for both profiles, with the division shown for each.
A recommendation to Meridian's launch director, defended using your D7 result, stating plainly what would have to change about either profile for your recommendation to flip.

balance.argument_a: The Fast-Track reaches the station in a small number of orbits, leaving the largest possible share of the vehicle's fixed autonomous-flight/consumables allowance untouched at docking (Appendix C). Real operational precedent (the modern 4-orbit/~6-hour and 2-orbit/~3-hour Soyuz profiles) shows this is the profile actually flown whenever launch conditions allow, precisely because it preserves the largest contingency reserve for a failed first approach or a docking hold-off -- a real, quantifiable safety and schedule-resilience margin.
balance.argument_b: The Phasing Climb tolerates a much wider range of initial phase angle, which means far more calendar days are workable launch attempts (Appendix D). Real orbital-mechanics precedent documents phasing-orbit rendezvous durations spanning roughly one to five days depending on how far off the phase angle starts at liftoff, because the vehicle can simply fly more or fewer phasing orbits to absorb the mismatch. A launch provider that can launch on far more of its scheduled days avoids the real, recurring cost of a scrubbed or slipped attempt (weather holds, range conflicts, technical delays).
balance.margin_basis: Primary metric: hours of autonomous-flight/consumables reserve remaining at docking (D4), divided by the number of days per 30-day launch calendar that fall inside that profile's workable phase-angle tolerance band (D6) -- a ratio of two independently-sourced quantities, not a single total. Once Appendix B's real modeled transit times, Appendix C's real total autonomous-flight allowance, and Appendix D's real (or literature-derived) phase-angle tolerance bands are sourced by case-research, compute: reserve_hours_remaining(profile) = total_allowance_hours - modeled_transit_hours(profile); workable_days_per_30(profile) = 30 * (phase_angle_tolerance_degrees(profile) / 360); metric(profile) = reserve_hours_remaining(profile) / workable_days_per_30(profile). Compare metric(A) vs metric(B) as a percent difference. This is expected, not yet confirmed, to land inside SPEC §2's ~20% cap because -- unlike the-transfer-window's ~800x chemical-vs-electric transit-time asymmetry -- both terms in this ratio are documented in real sources to differ by only a few-x between the two profiles (transit times of hours vs. days, not hours vs. months; phase-angle tolerances that both real profiles are specifically engineered to keep workable within a normal launch cadence).
